Flag Decoder
The Juneteenth flag is full of meaning. Tap each part to learn what it stands for.

Tap to reveal

Students interpret the symbols of the Juneteenth flag.
Draw the Juneteenth flag. Label one part and tell what it means.
The star
The star stands for Texas, where the last enslaved people in the Confederacy learned they were free. It also stands for freedom in all 50 states.
The burst around the star
The burst, like a new star in the sky (a nova), stands for a new beginning and a new freedom.
The arc (the curved line)
The arc is a new horizon — the hopes and chances ahead for free people.
Red, white, and blue
These are the colors of the U.S. flag. They show that enslaved people and their descendants were, and are, Americans.
The date June 19, 1865
Many flags add this date — the day freedom was announced in Galveston, Texas.
The Juneteenth flag was designed in 1997 by Ben Haith and illustrated by Lisa Jeanne Graf.

Identify: what do you see?
A community band and crowd gathered for an Emancipation Day celebration in Texas, June 19, 1900 — 35 years after the Galveston announcement.
Look closely: clothing and instruments
People wear their best clothes and carry brass instruments. Celebrations often included music, parades, speeches, and shared meals.
Understand: why a band?
Public music and gathering were ways formerly enslaved families and their descendants claimed freedom together, in public, with pride.

Many Texas communities still hold Juneteenth parades and music. What stays the same? What has changed?

Who she is
Opal Lee is a retired teacher from Fort Worth, Texas, born in 1926. People call her the “Grandmother of Juneteenth.”
Her idea
She wanted Juneteenth to be a national holiday so the whole country would remember emancipation.
Her walk
Starting at age 89, she walked 2.5 miles in cities across the country — 2.5 miles for the 2.5 years between the Emancipation Proclamation and the news reaching Galveston.
The petition
She gathered more than a million signatures asking Congress to act.
In 2021, Juneteenth became a federal holiday, and Opal Lee stood with the president as he signed the law.
Based on reporting about Opal Lee’s campaign for a Juneteenth national holiday.

Mark what the order announced, encouraged, and warned against.
Click to annotate

Students analyze General Order No. 3, distinguishing its declaration from its instructions, to explain social effects of the Civil War and Reconstruction in Texas.
The order announced freedom and equal rights. It also told freed people what to do and what not to do. In two sentences, explain the tension between the promise and the instructions.

Teach slavery and emancipation as central to U.S. history, not a side note. Use precise language — enslaved people, enslavers — and keep people, not systems alone, at the center. Center the agency of the freed, and examine the gap between freedom as law and freedom in practice. (Framework: Learning for Justice, Teaching Hard History.)
The people of Texas are informed that, in accordance with a proclamation from the Executive of the United States, all slaves are free.
This involves an absolute equality of personal rights and rights of property between former masters and slaves,
and the connection heretofore existing between them becomes that between employer and hired labor.
The freedmen are advised to remain quietly at their present homes and work for wages.
They are informed that they will not be allowed to collect at military posts,
and that they will not be supported in idleness either there or elsewhere.

“The people of Texas are informed that, in accordance with a proclamation from the Executive of the United States, all slaves are free. This involves an absolute equality of personal rights and rights of property between former masters and slaves, and the connection heretofore existing between them becomes that between employer and hired labor. The freedmen are advised to remain quietly at their present homes and work for wages. They are informed that they will not be allowed to collect at military posts and that they will not be supported in idleness either there or elsewhere.”
General Order No. 3, Headquarters District of Texas, Galveston, June 19, 1865, issued by Major General Gordon Granger. U.S. National Archives.
National Archives · General Order No. 3
Texas History for Teachers · Texas Today lesson (UNT)
Announced: “all slaves are free” and “an absolute equality of personal rights and rights of property.”
Encouraged: the relationship becomes “employer and hired labor”; freed people are “advised to remain quietly… and work for wages.”
Warned: they “will not be allowed to collect at military posts” and “will not be supported in idleness.”
The order promised “absolute equality,” then told freed people to stay and work for wages. Why might that feel like a mixed message?
Who benefited from freed people remaining on the same farms?
Freedom was announced in Texas 2.5 years after the Emancipation Proclamation. Why did the news take so long?

Document-based inquiry
analyze a document, qualify a claim with evidence, and state a limitation.
Students construct an evidence-based interpretation of the meaning of freedom in June 1865.
Write a thesis: did General Order No. 3 deliver freedom, or a conditional freedom? Use two clauses as evidence, and name one limitation of relying on this single document.
all slaves are free.
the connection heretofore existing between them becomes that between employer and hired labor.
they will not be allowed to collect at military posts,
Promise: “all slaves are free”; “an absolute equality of personal rights and rights of property.”
Limit: recasting the relationship as “employer and hired labor”; “remain quietly… and work for wages”; no gathering at military posts; no support “in idleness.”
A strong response notes that true equality required the 13th and 14th Amendments and enforcement that this order alone did not guarantee.

The Holiday Case
Lawmakers weigh evidence before they act. Work through each question to assemble the strongest case for Juneteenth as a national holiday. A correct choice opens the next step.
Build the evidence-based case for why Juneteenth became a federal holiday.
Evidence-based argument
select evidence and build a reasoned historical argument.
Students construct an evidence-based argument that anticipates a counterargument.
Write a one-paragraph argument — claim, two pieces of evidence, and a response to one counterargument — on why Juneteenth became a federal holiday in 2021.
Step 1 — Which is a thesis a historian could defend with evidence?
Choose the defensible claim.
Juneteenth marks the end of enforced slavery in the last Confederate state and belongs in the national memory of emancipation.
Juneteenth is simply the best holiday.
Everyone enjoys a day off.
A thesis makes a specific, defensible claim.
Step 2 — Which evidence best supports making Juneteenth national, not only in Texas?
Choose the strongest evidence.
Emancipation was a national event; the 13th Amendment ended slavery across the whole country in 1865.
Texas has good weather in June.
Opal Lee happens to be from Texas.
Strong evidence ties the local event to a national meaning.
Step 3 — Which counterargument should the case answer?
Choose the serious objection.
Some argue freedom was already law in 1863, so June 19 is only symbolic.
Some argue June is too hot for a holiday.
A strong argument anticipates and answers real objections.
Step 4 — Why commemorate June 19 even though emancipation was law in 1863?
Choose the best response to the counterargument.
It marks when freedom was finally enforced for the last enslaved people — the gap between law and reality.
There is no good reason; it is purely symbolic.
Commemoration marks enforcement and memory, not only the date a law passed.
Based on the DocsTeach Juneteenth General Order lesson and the National Archives.
Thesis: Juneteenth marks the enforcement of emancipation in the last Confederate state and belongs in national memory.
Evidence: emancipation was national; the 13th Amendment (1865) ended slavery everywhere.
Counterargument answered: though freedom was law in 1863, June 19 marks when it was finally enforced — the gap between law and reality.

Why is answering a counterargument part of a strong argument?
